tldr: This study is the world's first to demonstrate a humanoid robot jumping onto monkey bars, brachiating across them, and landing safely on hardware, relying solely on raw point clouds from a head-mounted solid-state lidar.
hero_caption: Hardware demonstrations on the PM-01 humanoid: jumping onto monkey bars (top left) and ducking under a thin overhead obstacle (top right). Bottom: attention weights over the raw lidar scan, clearly showing that visual attention focuses sharply on task-critical features like thin bars and obstacles.
overview:
Intermediate representations such as elevation maps and voxel grids have long been standard for legged robot perception. However, elevation maps discard overhead overhangs and thin structures, while voxel grids suffer from exploding computational costs at high resolutions. Direct raw point-cloud methods, on the other hand, have mostly been applied to large obstacles or uneven terrain; dynamic whole-body tasks requiring precise contact with centimeter-thin structures have remained uncharted territory.

To tackle this, the authors chose monkey-bar traversal (brachiation) as an extreme benchmark. The robot must leap to thin bars, swing forward rhythmically while suspended, and finally dismount to land safely—a formidable challenge demanding fine perception, contact exploration, and peak whole-body dynamic capability simultaneously. To solve it, they designed an end-to-end control policy that couples an attention mechanism processing the raw solid-state lidar grid with a recurrent memory (GRU). Training relies on a phase-scheduled distillation pipeline that combines privileged expert policies for each subtask into a single student policy, followed by PPO fine-tuning.

To ensure successful sim-to-real transfer, the authors physically modeled battery-voltage sag from sudden load spikes, actuator thermal limits, and lidar-specific beam divergence noise (edge bleed) directly inside the simulator. The humanoid was also equipped with custom passive hook end-effectors that allow releasing bars without requiring high torques.

Evaluated on the PM-01 humanoid hardware across three bar configurations differing in height and spacing, the robot completed the full jump-up -> brachiation -> jump-down sequence in 14 out of 15 trials (a 93% success rate). It reached brachiation speeds up to 0.5 m/s, comparable to human speeds. Furthermore, the exact same perception backbone enabled a separately trained policy to duck beneath 2 cm thin overhead obstacles without code changes, demonstrating strong generality.
contributions: Proposed an attention-based end-to-end control system that perceives thin 3D structures directly from raw solid-state lidar scans to execute jump-up, brachiation, and jump-down.
Developed a distillation pipeline that integrates multiple privileged task experts into a single perceptive student policy via phase scheduling and PopArt-style advantage normalization.
Constructed high-fidelity sim-to-real models for battery-voltage sag, actuator thermal buildup, and lidar beam divergence noise, all crucial under extreme dynamic motions.
Demonstrated a 93% success rate across monkey-bar sequences with speeds up to 0.5 m/s on a real humanoid, and validated the same perception backbone on ducking beneath thin overhead obstacles.

sections.heading: Why make a humanoid tackle monkey bars?
sections.summary: Conventional intermediate representations like elevation maps and voxel grids struggle to capture thin overhead structures like monkey bars. This work breaks through this barrier by feeding raw lidar point clouds directly into an attention mechanism, autonomously controlling the full sequence from jumping up to brachiating and landing.
sections.details:
Robot-centric 2.5D elevation maps are widely used for legged robot navigation. While computationally lightweight and practical, they have a critical flaw: they completely miss overhead overhangs and thin structures like bars. On the other hand, full 3D voxel grids demand prohibitive memory and computation if the resolution is raised high enough to resolve thin bars.

Map-free approaches that feed raw depth images or point clouds directly into policies have recently emerged, but they have primarily targeted uneven ground and large obstacle avoidance. Extreme dynamic tasks requiring millisecond-level contact synchronization with centimeter-thin structures remained unexplored.

Monkey-bar traversal (brachiation) was chosen as the ultimate benchmark to test this challenge. It poses three major hurdles:
- The perceptual difficulty of extracting task-relevant geometry from sparse lidar returns with only a few hits per thin bar
- Exploring complex contact sequences: leaping to grasp, swinging to the next bar, and releasing to land
- Severe hardware constraints balanced between peak explosive power output and thermal limits

The authors overcame all three hurdles simultaneously by combining an attention-based raw point-cloud encoder, phase-scheduled distillation from privileged experts, and faithful sim-to-real modeling of battery and thermal dynamics.

captions.F1: Hardware snapshots of monkey-bar jumping and obstacle ducking (top), paired with corresponding attention weights over raw lidar scans (bottom). Visual attention selectively and distinctly concentrates on the bars to grasp or obstacles posing collision hazards among dense point clouds.

sections.heading: Where perceptive locomotion, privileged distillation, and dynamic traversal stand today
sections.summary: This section reviews advances in raw-sensor perceptive locomotion and privileged distillation while highlighting the novelty of this work. Key differentiators include establishing contact with thin airborne structures using onboard sensing alone and employing phase-scheduled distillation aligned with task progress.
sections.details:
This work stands at the intersection of four main research areas:

- Perceptive Locomotion: Recent studies in quadrupedal and humanoid parkour have actively utilized raw depth camera or lidar data. However, these targets have mostly been large boxes or uneven ground; none have handled the precision required for whole-body contact targeting centimeter-thin bars as in this work.
- Privileged Distillation: Training a privileged "teacher" with full state information in simulation and distilling it to a "student" observing only realistic sensor inputs via imitation learning (such as DAgger) is a standard approach. While prior work has combined or switched multiple skills, this work switches the active teacher based on task progression (phases) within a single episode and normalizes advantages per phase, smoothly blending skills with disparate reward scales into a single policy.
- Sim-to-Real Modeling: Precise actuator modeling is essential for dynamic motions on hardware. This work goes a step further by modeling instantaneous battery-voltage drops (sag) caused by high current draw, motor winding heat accumulation, and specific noise artifacts from lidar beam divergence.
- Dynamic Traversal and Brachiation: While prior brachiation research relied on specialized multi-link mechanisms or assumed known bar coordinates, no general-purpose humanoid had previously achieved the full sequence—jumping up, brachiating, and landing—relying solely on its own head-mounted sensors.

sections.heading: Wrist-twist release hooks and distortion-free solid-state lidar
sections.summary: The hardware uses the PM-01 humanoid, equipped with newly designed passive hook end-effectors that endure dynamic loads while disengaging smoothly. The head houses a solid-state lidar that resists scanning distortion during vigorous body motion.
sections.details:
Pragmatic hardware engineering made these punishing monkey-bar maneuvers viable.

### III-A Passive Hook End-Effectors
Instead of articulated robotic hands, simple passive hooks waterjet-cut from stainless steel plates were adopted for grasping bars (Fig. F3(a)). This design serves clear purposes:
- Load and Impact Durability: Withstands the dynamic swings supporting robot self-weight and landing impacts.
- Tolerance to Positional Error: A wide 60 mm opening reliably catches bars with 1–3 cm radii even under contact inaccuracies.
- Low-Torque Release: Instead of lifting the entire body upward to unhook, the policy rotates the wrist-yaw axis to slide the hook outward horizontally (Fig. F3(b)). This drastically cuts motor load during disengagement and prevents thermal shutdown. In addition, its front-back symmetric shape naturally accommodates both forward and backward traversal modes (Fig. F3(c)).

### III-B Head-Mounted Solid-State Lidar
For external sensing, a RoboSense E1R was chosen. It features a wide FOV ($120^\circ$ horizontal, $90^\circ$ vertical) and a dense $192 \times 144$ scan pattern. Solid-state lidar was favored over mechanical spinning lidar because its electronic scanning eliminates rolling-shutter geometric distortions during violent dynamic swings. A subsampled subset of this dense scan is fed to the control policy at 10 Hz.

captions.F3: Modified PM-01 hardware with hook end-effectors and head-mounted lidar (a). Passive bar release achieved by simply rotating the wrist yaw (b), and backward traversal enabled by the hook's front-back symmetry (c).

sections.heading: Unifying three expert teachers into a single perceptive student
sections.summary: Three privileged experts (jump-up, brachiation, jump-down) that know exact bar coordinates are trained via RL and distilled into a single student policy scheduled by phase. An attention encoder preserving the raw scan grid and a GRU memory underpin its perception.
sections.details:
The learning framework is divided into privileged teacher training and multi-stage distillation to a perceptive student (Fig. F4).

### IV-B & C Privileged Teacher Training and Curricula
First, privileged experts that observe 3D bar endpoint coordinates directly are trained via PPO. The task is split into three phases—Jump-up, Brachiation, and Jump-down—trained as independent MLP policies. Jump-up and jump-down use contact-target rewards and a ladder-height curriculum, while brachiation uses a curriculum that widens bar spacing and narrows bar width.

### IV-D Reward Design and Physical Limits
A shared reward block enforces soft joint limit protection and total limb torque limits, alongside penalties for battery-voltage sag and motor heating described later. This naturally encourages physically plausible motions that avoid damaging the hardware.

### IV-E Three-Stage Multi-Teacher Distillation Pipeline
To fuse the three teachers into a single student, a three-stage distillation pipeline switches between active teachers according to task progression (phase):
- Stage 1 (Pure Imitation): Using DAgger, the student clones the active teacher's actions with MSE loss.
- Stage 2 (Critic Warm-Up): To prevent catastrophic collapse when transitioning to RL, action cloning continues while the critic (value function) is trained on GAE returns alone.
- Stage 3 (Regularized PPO): Transitions to PPO reinforcement learning while gradually decaying the imitation loss anchor. Because reward scales vary across phases, advantage normalization inspired by PopArt is applied per phase, preventing any single phase from dominating gradient updates.

### IV-F & G Perceptive Architecture and Auxiliary Loss
Rather than treating the lidar scan as an unordered set, the student policy feeds the scan into an attention mechanism (AME-2) while preserving its 2D grid structure. Extracted features are concatenated with proprioception (joint positions, velocities, IMU) and passed to a GRU memory for temporal integration. To accelerate distillation, an auxiliary task predicting the 3D position and orientation of the nearest bar centerline from the GRU hidden state is jointly trained.

captions.F4: Overall system architecture: (A) three subtask teachers trained independently with privileged information, (B) the student model processing raw lidar scans in grid form via attention and GRU, and (C) the three-stage distillation pipeline connecting behavioral cloning to PPO fine-tuning.

sections.heading: Thorough modeling of voltage sag, motor heating, and lidar noise
sections.summary: Battery-voltage drops and actuator thermal accumulation—the primary causes of real-world hardware failure—were formulated in simulation. Additionally, a noise model faithfully captures beam divergence artifacts (edge bleed) prominent around thin structures.
sections.details:
Policies that work in simulation are futile if they fail or break down on real hardware. This work rigorously models three critical phenomena occurring at physical limits:

### V-A Battery and Thermal Modeling
- Battery-Voltage Sag: When total joint torque $\sum |\tau|$ surges, heavy current draw causes terminal voltage to drop sharply. This is modeled via a first-order lag filter, degrading available motor torque and maximum velocity in real time proportionally to the voltage ratio. Without this, the robot suffered brownouts from overcurrent during jumping. Incorporating a voltage sag penalty into the reward eliminated brownouts completely on hardware.
- Actuator Thermal Model: During monkey-bar suspension, shoulder and elbow joints operate near torque limits, heating up rapidly. A leaky integrator tracking load was introduced as a proxy for winding temperature in simulation. Sustained high loads incur penalties, compelling the policy to spontaneously discover efficient passive hanging and weight-shifting strategies.

### V-B & C Lidar Noise and Edge Bleed Replication
When measuring thin bars with solid-state lidar, beam divergence ($0.625^\circ$ cone) splits rays at bar edges, scattering returns behind the target—a phenomenon known as edge bleed or the mixed-pixel effect (Fig. F6(a)).
For training, a fast Warp-based stochastic noise model was developed to blend background depths based on edge detection (Fig. F6(b)). For validation in MuJoCo, a high-fidelity model casts 16 rays per pixel within the cone and composites them via the inverse-square law, synthesizing point clouds virtually indistinguishable from real-world scans (Fig. F6(c)).

captions.F6: Lidar point-cloud noise observed on real hardware (a), compared with replications in the training simulator (b) and validation simulator (c). Step-boundary artifacts caused by finite beam divergence (cones) shown on the far right (d) are accurately reproduced.

sections.heading: 93% success rate and 0.5 m/s on hardware, extended to obstacle ducking
sections.summary: After ablation studies confirmed the superiority of the attention mechanism and auxiliary loss, monkey-bar traversal was executed on the PM-01 robot. It succeeded in 14 of 15 trials, reaching a human-like 0.5 m/s. The same perception backbone also achieved a 100% success rate ducking under 2 cm thin bars.
sections.details:
Encoder comparisons, cross-simulator evaluations, and hardware experiments were conducted to validate the approach.

### VI-A Ablations on Encoders and Auxiliary Loss
Comparing behavioral cloning loss (BC loss) in early distillation revealed that the proposed attention-based encoder (AME-2) achieved the lowest loss across all phases, despite having roughly one order of magnitude fewer parameters than CNNs and two orders fewer than MLPs. Adding the auxiliary centerline prediction loss (CL) further reduced loss across all encoders, proving that explicit geometric guidance strongly aids temporal feature extraction.

### VI-B & C Real-World Traversal and Ducking
Hardware tests were performed on the PM-01 humanoid across three monkey-bar setups with varying bar heights and spacings.
- Monkey-Bar Traversal Sequence: The robot starts stationary beneath the bars and operates fully autonomously once given a single target coordinate by the operator. The overall success rate reached 14 out of 15 trials (93%). The single failure occurred when the hook failed to advance to the next bar after a successful jump. The policy operated robustly even on flexible, swaying rig structures that bend under human weight, reaching a peak brachiation speed of 0.5 m/s, demonstrating agility comparable to humans (Fig. F2).
- Obstacle Ducking: Using the exact same perception encoder, a separate policy trained to duck under overhead bars was tested on hardware. Facing wooden bars with cross-sections of only 2 cm × 2 cm set at unknown angles (clearances of 1.0–1.3 m), the robot successfully ducked and passed beneath them in 10 out of 10 trials without a single collision (Fig. F7).

captions.F2: Hardware monkey-bar traversal sequence executed by the learned perceptive controller. Jumping from the ground, swinging rhythmically between bars, and final safe landing are seamlessly connected.
captions.F7: Photo sequence of the humanoid ducking beneath a thin wooden obstacle (cross-section 2 cm, height 1.2 m), recognized in real time via lidar as the robot lowers its posture to pass through.

sections.heading: Summary and outlook: raw point clouds unlock whole-body dynamics
sections.summary: This work demonstrates that acrobatic whole-body contact dynamics can be achieved directly from raw head-mounted lidar point clouds and rigorous hardware limit modeling. Future directions include adapting to diverse environments and handling partially observed structures requiring long-term memory.
sections.details:
This study showed that highly dynamic, acrobatic whole-body motions can be generated directly from raw solid-state lidar data without relying on elevation maps. Key to this success were an attention mechanism capable of focusing on thin geometry, and uncompromising modeling of hardware limits such as battery-voltage sag, thermal buildup, and lidar beam divergence. Furthermore, applying the same perception backbone directly to overhead obstacle avoidance highlights the versatility of raw point-cloud processing.

However, policies are currently trained separately for each task, and generalization to irregular structures beyond straight ladders remains to be verified. Future work aims to develop visual navigation integrated with persistent 3D spatial memory, enabling humanoids to approach and interact with structures that have slipped out of view into blind spots for extended durations.

takeaways: For airborne geometry that disappears in elevation maps—such as thin bars or overhangs—applying attention while preserving the raw point cloud's 2D grid structure is remarkably effective.

When transferring explosive dynamic motions (like jumping) to real humanoids, modeling both battery-voltage sag and actuator thermal accumulation in simulation is essential to avoid frequent brownouts or shutdowns.
Disparate sub-skills can be stably integrated into a single student policy by combining a phase schedule tied to task progress with PopArt-style advantage normalization.
Solid-state lidar's edge bleed noise from beam divergence can be successfully bridged for sim-to-real transfer using a lightweight stochastic background-blending model.
limitations: While the perception backbone architecture is shared between monkey-bar traversal and obstacle ducking, policies are trained separately per task rather than switching dynamically within a single unified policy.
Evaluations were restricted to straight, evenly spaced monkey bars; generalization to highly irregular 3D jungle gyms or curved configurations has not yet been demonstrated.
Tracking bars once they pass overhead out of view relies solely on the GRU's short-term memory, lacking a persistent long-term spatial memory map for sustained blind spots.
